clue.text: A copper car going free in China

explanation.surface: A police car speeds loose through a Chinese city.
explanation.walkthrough: A PANDA car was the British name for a small police patrol car, once painted in black-and-white panels; the second reading is the giant bear living wild in China.
explanation.definitionFit: Police patrol cars were nicknamed after the black-and-white bear for their livery, and that bear roams wild only in Chinese forests.

clue.text: Ref caught up in new peril because he takes things in a petty way?

definitions.text: he takes things in a petty way?

indicators.note: the reversed referee sits inside the reworked letters of peril
new signals that the letters of peril are made afresh in another order
in a down clue, caught up has the word ref read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A football referee gets caught in fresh danger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught up' turns REF into FER, and 'in' puts it inside PILER, the letters of 'peril' rearranged ('new').
explanation.definitionFit: A petty thief steals small items, which is exactly what is meant by taking things in a small way.

clue.text: Blue ran out like a distant cloud

indicators.note: out suggests the letters of blue ran are put out of their order

explanation.surface: A blue dye ran, washing out like faraway mist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' reorders the seven letters of BLUE RAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A nebula is a vast cloud of gas and dust in deep space, and the adjective describes things relating to one.

clue.text: A wiry egoist has gone crooked

indicators.note: has gone says the self-centred letter has left the word wiry

parts.note: taken as written
an egoist is all about I, the first-person pronoun

explanation.surface: A lean, self-obsessed man has turned dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has gone' removes I (the egoist's favourite word) from WIRY, leaving WRY after A.
explanation.definitionFit: Something askew or out of true is bent, which is the sense of crooked here.

clue.text: Refuse corny food with wave of the arm

parts.note: bran is the husk sifted from grain, the leftover refuse of corn
a dish is a serving of food

explanation.surface: Someone waves away a plate of cereal they refuse to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb but is the noun: bran is what is left when corn is milled.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun this is a flourish, a showy waving movement made with a weapon or the hand.

clue.text: Regard esteem above skill

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: regard means respect
skill means ability

explanation.surface: A claim that reputation counts for more than talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'above' places RESPECT on top of ABILITY in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Being held in good standing by others, decent and well thought of, is what esteem amounts to.

clue.text: Pioneer zoologist turning up in Omaha on tour

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up has the run of letters read from bottom to top
in says the letters sit inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A celebrated naturalist is spotted touring Nebraska.
explanation.walkthrough: The run HAON inside 'omaHA ON tour' is read upwards ('turning up') after 'in' picks it out.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical ark-builder gathered animals two by two, making him the first collector of creatures.

clue.text: What a Spanish princess was called over a baby

definitions.text: What a Spanish princess was called

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece is written over the second

parts.note: a baby is an infant

explanation.surface: A princess in Spain was given a title when she was a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' puts INFANT above A in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The title was given to a daughter of a Spanish or Portuguese king who was not heir to the throne.

clue.text: Hellish shade!

indicators.note: hellish suggests a fiendish jumble, so the letters of shade are rearranged

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a ghost from the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hellish' rearranges SHADE; the whole clue also describes the place, since a shade is a ghost of the classical underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek underworld was the home of the dead, where ghosts known as shades wandered.

clue.text: Well acquainted with Manor, I hear, and its easy-going style

parts.note: well acquainted with something means familiar with it

indicators.note: I hear signals that the word manor is said out loud and spelt differently

parts.note: a manor is a country house and estate

explanation.surface: Someone who knows the big house well has a relaxed way about them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I hear' means MANOR is spoken, giving MANNER.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal, relaxed way of behaving is a casual style of conduct.

clue.text: First book that is about crooked liar going round republic

indicators.note: going round says the reworked liar letters surround the rest
crooked suggests the letters of liar are bent out of shape
about says the abbreviation for that is surrounds the book letter

parts.note: IE is the abbreviation of id est, meaning that is

indicators.note: first picks the opening letter of book

explanation.surface: A dishonest storyteller travels around a West African state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' gives B from book, 'about' puts I E round it for IBE, and 'going round' puts L-RIA (LIAR rearranged by 'crooked') round that.
explanation.definitionFit: The West African country is a republic founded by freed American slaves.

clue.text: Appointed establishment with a big stick

explanation.surface: A newly opened office is guarded by someone with a club.
explanation.walkthrough: Read first as having employees, then as carrying a staff, a stout stick.
explanation.definitionFit: An organisation supplied with employees is manned; someone carrying a long walking pole holds one.

clue.text: She's caught and turned by ballet dancer

indicators.note: turned has the run of letters read backwards
caught by says the letters are held inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A woman is grabbed and spun round by a ballet dancer.
explanation.walkthrough: ALLE inside 'bALLEt' is read backwards ('turned').
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name stands for any woman, as the pronoun she does.

clue.text: Equestrian corollary?

explanation.surface: A one-word puzzle about horse-riding and logic.
explanation.definitionFit: A horseman sits on a mount; a proposition's follow-on, or an added clause to a statement, is also called by this name.

clue.text: Our responsibility rests here

parts.note: split as two words the answer says the burden lies on ourselves, and as one word it is a duty

explanation.surface: A slogan accepting that the buck stops with us.
explanation.definitionFit: A duty or burden is a load of responsibility, and here it sits upon the speakers.

clue.text: Capital of Rhone and Loire destroyed Syon

annotationWithheld.why: Capital of Rhone and Loire destroyed Syon: L must come from 'Loire' via 'Capital of', which is also needed in the definition 'Capital of Rhone (and Loire)', so 'Capital of' does two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Capital of Rhone and Loire destroyed Syon

clue.text: "I'll sing thee songs of ——" (Wills)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from W. G. Wills's Victorian song lyric, set to music by Frederic Clay, naming a poetic word for Arabia

explanation.surface: A line from a Victorian parlour ballad with its last word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad's missing word is an old poetic name for Arabia, the land the singer promises to sing about.

clue.text: Victory in a real organisation for Sir Robert Peel, for example

indicators.note: organisation means the letters of victory in a real are arranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A political triumph within a genuine party structure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organisation' rearranges the fourteen letters of VICTORY IN A REAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Peel was prime minister in 1834 and 1841, at the start of the queen's long reign, so he is a figure from its first years.

clue.text: Guess I'm taken in by what Will left

indicators.note: taken in by says the letters of I'm are held inside the inheritance

parts.note: what a will leaves is a person's estate

explanation.surface: Someone guesses about what Will left them in his bequest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' looks like a man's name but is the legal document, and what it leaves is the ESTATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough calculation is an approximate guess.

clue.text: Are they forced to use 1's across for rural rides?

definitions.text: Are they forced to use 1's across for rural rides?

parts.words: Are they forced to use 1's across for rural rides?
parts.note: the police force in the countryside drives the black-and-white patrol cars of 1 across; forced plays on the police force

explanation.surface: A question about whether village people must ride in black-and-white bears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bobbies' is British slang for police officers; 'forced' puns on a police force, and 1 across gives the patrol car.
explanation.definitionFit: Village constables of a rural police force patrolled their beat in small patrol cars.

clue.text: Rhetoric for a congregation

explanation.surface: Speech-making to a church audience.
explanation.definitionFit: The art of public speaking is eloquence; a religious society of priests founded by St Philip Neri also takes this name.

clue.text: Confection composer made in the Arctic?

parts.note: an ice is a frozen sweet confection
Alban Berg was an Austrian composer

explanation.surface: A dessert named after a composer, frozen in the far north.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: the polar sea makes these floating masses.
explanation.definitionFit: Great floating chunks of frozen fresh water break off glaciers in polar seas.

clue.text: Hire purchase squeezing each battered old car

indicators.note: squeezing says the abbreviation for hire purchase holds the letters for each

parts.note: HP is the abbreviation for hire purchase, the British instalment-buying scheme

explanation.surface: Buying a wreck of a car on instalments.
explanation.walkthrough: Hire purchase (HP) is the British term for buying on instalments.
explanation.definitionFit: A jalopy or wreck of a vehicle is slangily called a pile, as in a pile of junk.

clue.text: Socked, and sprayed down

explanation.surface: Someone is punched and then doused with water.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing stockings or tights means being in hose; washing with a garden pipe is another meaning.

clue.text: Recover from a series of blows in court

definitions.text: a series of blows in court

explanation.surface: A boxer bounces back after taking punches in the ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The court is a tennis court, where a long exchange of shots is a rally.
explanation.definitionFit: To revive or regain strength is one meaning; a long exchange of shots in tennis is the other.

clue.text: The other half is for the neighbours

definitions.text: The other half is for the neighbours

parts.words: The other half is for the neighbours
parts.note: describes a house built as one of a joined pair, where the other half is the home next door

explanation.surface: A remark that one's partner is meant for the people next door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The other half' looks like a spouse; it is the adjoining half of a semi-detached house, a common British pair of joined homes.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-detached house shares one wall with its neighbour's twin home.

clue.text: Ship's company boasted thus

explanation.surface: The sailors bragged about themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel's sailors form its complement; the past tense of crow, to brag, is the second sense.

clue.text: A simple growth?

parts.note: a simple is an old word for a medicinal plant, so a simple growth is a plant used in remedies

explanation.surface: A doctor's question about whether a lump is harmless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'growth' suggests a tumour; 'simple' is a noun here, the old name for a healing plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Healers once called a single medicinal plant a simple, and such plants are culinary and medicinal greenery.

clue.text: A Scotsman's pouch that could attract the moths, some say!

definitions.text: A Scotsman's pouch that could attract the moths, some say!

parts.words: A Scotsman's pouch that could attract the moths, some say!
parts.note: the furry pouch worn with a kilt, which a stingy Scot rarely opens, so moths are said to live in it

explanation.surface: A jibe that a Scotsman's purse is so rarely opened that moths move in.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the old stereotype of the tight-fisted Scot: money never leaves the pouch, so moths fly out when it is opened.
explanation.definitionFit: The fur purse hung in front of a kilt is the Highland dress pouch.

clue.text: There's a bigger batch of letters for Tess

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone notes a longer name hides behind a short nickname.
explanation.walkthrough: The rest of the clue says the full name has more letters than its short form.
explanation.definitionFit: The short form of the woman's name is its diminutive, as Liz is for Elizabeth.

clue.text: Labour from dawn to dusk?

parts.note: a full stint of work lasting the hours of daylight

explanation.surface: A question about working all the daylight hours.
explanation.definitionFit: A full shift of toil lasting the hours of daylight is a standard unit of work.

clue.text: Leading general in blue make-up should rouse the troops!

indicators.note: in places the general's first letter inside the reworked blue
make-up suggests the letters of blue are made up into a new order
leading picks the first letter of general

explanation.surface: A top general wearing blue cosmetics is meant to stir the soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading' gives G, and 'in' puts it inside BULE, the letters of 'blue' rearranged ('make-up').
explanation.definitionFit: The brass horn sounds reveille to wake soldiers, so it is the instrument that rouses them.
